questions.qtext:
Let \( S = \{a,b\} \) be an alphabet, with total order \( a < b \). Let \( \Sigma = S^* \) be the set of all strings over \( S \); for \( w = s_1 s_2 \ldots s_n \in \Sigma \) we write \( \ell(w) = n \), and for \( 1 \le r \le n = \ell(w) \) we write \( w_r = s_1 s_2 \ldots s_r \). Denote by \( \varepsilon \) the unique word of \( \Sigma \) such that \( \ell(\varepsilon) = 0 \), the null string. Conventionally \( w_0 = \varepsilon \) for all words \( w \in \Sigma \).

Define relation \( \prec \) on \( \Sigma \) as follows:

Let \( v, w \in \Sigma \), and \( n = \min\{\ell(v), \ell(w)\} \). Let \( r = \max\{\, i \mid v_i = w_i \,\} \le n \).

Then \( v \prec w \) if:

either (i) \( \ell(v) = r \);

or (ii) \( v_{r+1} = v_r a,\; w_{r+1} = w_r b \), where \( v_r = w_r \).

Which of following conditions are satisfied by \( (\Sigma, \prec) \)? (Select all that apply)

\[ \begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Process 1} & \text{Process 2} & \text{Process 3} \\ \hline \\[1pt] \begin{aligned}[t] &\hspace{1.5em}\texttt{Loop1:} \\ &\hspace{4em}\texttt{P(a);} \\ &\hspace{4em}\texttt{print("H");} \\ &\hspace{4em}\texttt{print("E");} \\ &\hspace{4em}\texttt{V(b);} \\ &\hspace{4em}\texttt{BLANK} \\ &\hspace{4em}\texttt{goto Loop1;} \end{aligned} & \begin{aligned}[t] &\hspace{1.5em}\texttt{Loop2:} \\ &\hspace{4em}\texttt{P(b);} \\ &\hspace{4em}\texttt{print("L");} \\ &\hspace{4em}\texttt{BLANK} \\ &\hspace{4em}\texttt{goto Loop2;} \end{aligned} & \begin{aligned}[t] &\hspace{1.5em}\texttt{Loop3:} \\ &\hspace{4em}\texttt{BLANK} \\ &\hspace{4em}\texttt{print("O");} \\ &\hspace{4em}\texttt{goto Loop3;} \end{aligned} \end{array} \]

Consider the following recursive function:

What is the maximum height to which the recursion stack grows when the outermost call is \( f(10) \)? Assume that the stack is empty just before this outermost call.

\( \begin{aligned} &\texttt{struct node \{} \\ &\quad \texttt{int cval;} \\ &\quad \texttt{struct node *next;} \\ &\texttt{\}} \end{aligned} \)

\( \begin{aligned} &\texttt{main()} \\ &\texttt{\{} \\ &\quad \texttt{struct node N1, N2, N3;} \\ &\quad \texttt{N1.cval = 1; N2.cval = 10; N3.cval = 100;} \\ &\quad \texttt{N1.next = &N2; N2.next = &N3; N3.next = &N1;} \\ &\quad \texttt{printf("%d,%d", N2.next -> cval, N2.next -> next -> cval);} \\ &\texttt{\}} \end{aligned} \)

Consider the linked list shown below, with head pointing to the first node. Here, link denotes a pointer type to a node of the linked list (i.e., a typedef for struct node *).

$\texttt{1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → NULL}$

The following code segment is executed:

$\begin{aligned} &\texttt{link head, q, p;} \\ &\texttt{q = NULL;} \\ &\texttt{while (head != NULL)} \\ &\texttt{\{} \\ &\quad \texttt{p = head;} \\ &\quad \texttt{head = head->next;} \\ &\quad \texttt{p->next = q;} \\ &\quad \texttt{q = p;} \\ &\texttt{\}} \end{aligned}$

What is the final linked list after the execution of the above code?

Initially, $S_1$ (top $\rightarrow$ bottom) contains:

$$ S_1 = [1, 2, 3] $$

A mysterious procedure is executed as follows:

$$ \begin{aligned} &\texttt{MysteriousMove(S1, S2):} \\ &\quad \texttt{if S1 is empty:} \\ &\qquad \texttt{return} \\ &\quad \texttt{x <- Pop(S1)} \\ &\quad \texttt{MysteriousMove(S1, S2)} \\ &\quad \texttt{Push(S2, x)} \end{aligned} $$

After the call MysteriousMove(S1, S2) completes, the content of $S_2$ (from top $\rightarrow$ bottom) is:

questions.qtext:
Consider an undirected graph \( G = (V, E) \) and a subset \( S \subseteq V \). We say that an element \( u \in S \) is reachable from a different element \( v \in S \) if there exists a path between \( u \) and \( v \) in \( G \).

Design an algorithm to determine whether there exist two distinct vertices in \( S \) such that one is reachable from the other. Your algorithm should run in time \( O(|V| + |E|) \).

Which of the following algorithms satisfies the above requirement?

options.text: Compute all-pairs shortest paths in \( G \), and check whether any two vertices in \( S \) have a finite distance between them.
For each vertex \( s \in S \), run a DFS starting from \( s \) and check whether any other vertex of \( S \) is visited.

Compute the connected components of \( G \). For each connected component, count how many vertices from \( S \) it contains, and return true if any component contains at least two vertices from \( S \).
Sort the vertices of \( S \) by degree and check whether any two consecutive vertices are adjacent.

Consider the following statements related to shortest path algorithms.

Select all statements that are correct.

options.text: For all weighted graphs and all vertices \(s\) and \(t\), Bellman–Ford starting at \(s\) will always return a shortest path to \(t\).
If all edges in a graph have distinct weights, then the shortest path between two vertices is unique.
At the termination of the Bellman–Ford algorithm, even if the graph has a negative-length cycle, a correct shortest path is found for a vertex for which the shortest path is well-defined.

Given a graph \(G = (V, E)\) with positive edge weights, the Bellman–Ford algorithm and Dijkstra’s algorithm can produce different shortest-path trees despite always producing the same shortest-path weights.

questions.qtext:
Assume a Go-Back-N (GBN) sender and receiver. The receiver acknowledges each data segment with a cumulative ACK indicating the next expected data segment. Furthermore, it saves out-of-order segments in a buffer. The sender and receiver buffer can contain four segments each. The timeout period is much larger than the time required for the sender to transmit four segments in a row.

The sender wants to transmit \(10\) data segments numbered \(0,1,\ldots,9\) to the receiver. Assume that exactly one data segment is lost.

Select all statements that are correct.

options.text: In the <em>best case</em>, the sender transmits a total of \(11\) data segments.
In the <em>best case</em>, the lost data segment is segment \(0\).
In the <em>worst case</em>, the sender transmits a total of \(14\) data segments.
In the <em>worst case</em>, loss of an early data segment (for example, segment \(1\)) causes retransmission of all data segments in the current window.

Consider \(32\)-bit IPv4 addresses.

The routing table is given below.

\[ \begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \text{IP Prefix} & \text{Output Port} \\ \hline 00\ldots & \text{Port }4 \\ \hline 01\ldots & \text{Port }3 \\ \hline 010\ldots & \text{Port }5 \\ \hline 0111\ldots & \text{Port }9 \\ \hline 11\ldots & \text{Port }2 \\ \hline 00\ldots00 & \text{Port }8 \\ \hline \end{array} \]

How many \(32\)-bit IPv4 addresses are forwarded along Port \(3\)?

Reminder: \( 2^k - 2^{k-1} = 2^{k-1} \)
